14	CASE OD2-HO-KNOWN-2 (KNOWN, organizational): First-contact resolution drop at Thornlea Energy's Breckmouth contact centre
15	Setting: Thornlea Energy is a fictional regional energy supplier. Its single contact centre at Breckmouth has about 205 phone agents in 17 teams and handles roughly 21,500 inbound calls a week about billing, payments, tariffs, moving home and meters. Over-limit or complex billing cases go to a separate back-office Billing Resolution team (BRT). Several changes landed in the centre during April.
16	Presenting request: The Chief Operating Officer asks: first-contact resolution (FCR) was about 75% in Q1 and has been about 67% since late April. Why did it fall, and should the Head of Customer Operations' September plan go ahead, or should something else be done?
17	INITIAL EVIDENCE
18	E1 [stage S1] Email from Marisol Pentreath, Head of Customer Operations, to Gareth Linde, COO, 8 August (leadership-account): Gareth, FCR has gone from 75% in Q1 to 67% for May–July and I want to be straight about why. We put 38 new starters on the phones on 14 April, the biggest intake we have ever run, and the dashboard fell off a cliff the same week. Tenured teams haven't changed what they do. The tariff rise hasn't helped either: those calls are long and messy. My plan is to extend nesting for the April intake and, from September, put anyone below 65% FCR on a performance plan. I'd also like to pause the IVR supplier's phase-two work until we're stable.
19	E2 [stage S1] FCR dashboard extract, weekly site figures, produced by Planning (telemetry): Definition: an inbound call counts as resolved if the same account makes no further inbound contact (phone, chat or email) within 7 days, for any reason. Week commencing, FCR (every week to 19 May, then fortnightly): 17 Mar 75.2%; 24 Mar 74.9%; 31 Mar 75.1%; 7 Apr 74.8%; 14 Apr 70.3%; 21 Apr 67.5%; 28 Apr 67.1%; 5 May 67.4%; 12 May 66.9%; 19 May 67.3%; 2 Jun 67.0%; 16 Jun 67.2%; 30 Jun 67.1%. Inbound calls per week ranged from 20,800 to 22,600, except w/c 31 Mar (24,100). Q1 average 75.0%; May–Jul average 67.1%. This dashboard has no agent-level or contact-reason view.
20	E3 [stage S1] Operations change calendar, Q2 extract, maintained by Planning (document): 1 Apr: annual tariff increase takes effect (customer letters sent 3–14 Mar). 3 Apr: CRM release R24.3 (address lookup fix; new wrap-up codes). 14 Apr: April intake (38 agents) live on phones after six weeks' training and two weeks' nesting. 14 Apr: Finance credit-handling controls update, ref FC-0417, applied in the billing platform; Finance advised 'no agent training required'. 28 Apr: IVR menu redesign live (seven options reduced to five). 2 Jun: summer shift pattern begins. Planning note: items owned outside Customer Operations are listed for awareness only; their impact has not been assessed.
21	E4 [stage S1] Agent pulse survey, June: six free-text comments selected by the survey team as 'representative' from 141 responses (anonymous-staff-survey): 1) 'The new IVR dumps people in the wrong queue and they're cross before I've said hello.' 2) 'Half the April lot still transfer anything they don't know.' 3) 'Since the price rise every call is an argument.' 4) 'I used to just sort out a wrong bill. Now half of them go off to BRT and the customer rings back.' 5) 'No breathing space between calls any more, occupancy is through the roof.' 6) 'Team leaders only care about handle time.'
22	E5 [stage S1] Complaints log, monthly summary, Customer Relations (system-record): Complaints per 10,000 contacts: Jan 40, Feb 42, Mar 41, Apr 47, May 50, Jun 49, Jul 50. The complaint category field is optional on the logging form, and 64% of complaints since January are uncategorised. Of categorised complaints for April–July, the largest category is 'Price/tariff' (31%), followed by 'Service – delay' (24%) and 'Billing accuracy' (19%). Complaints are counted by the month received, not linked to the originating call.
23	E6 [stage S1] Notes of conversation with Lewis Abara, team leader for the April-intake nesting group, 6 August (manager-account): 'My twelve are hitting handle time and their QA is improving week by week. I can't tell you their FCR. The dashboard only gives the site number, and MI produce agent-level FCR only on request. Honestly, on the floor they don't look much different to my old hands, but that's my impression, not data. I'd be gutted if they went on performance plans for a site-wide number.'
24	CATALOGUE (full contents)
25	C1 [stage S1] Learning & Development training records and assessment results, April intake and prior two intakes - Learning & Development team (document): April intake (38 agents): six-week classroom programme plus two weeks' supervised nesting, same syllabus as the October and January intakes. Final assessment pass rate: April 92% (35/38 first attempt; 3 passed on resit); October 90%; January 94%. The billing module covers reading bills, explaining estimated reads and applying adjustments 'within the agent's system authority'. Trainer comment: 'Strong cohort, a little more nervous on the phones than January.' L&D holds no performance measures after agents go live on the floor.
26	C2 [stage S1] IVR supplier go-live report and routing statistics, 28 April–30 June - Calloway Voice Systems (IVR supplier), report dated 30 June (vendor-account): Menu reduced from seven to five options on 28 April. Menu completion 94% (previously 91%). Calls transferred between queues within 60 seconds of answer, used as a proxy for misrouting: 3.8% in May–June vs 4.0% in Feb–March. Average time in menu 41s vs 58s. Supplier comment: 'The redesign is performing well; phase two (natural-language routing) should proceed as planned.' The report covers IVR metrics only. The supplier does not receive FCR data.
27	C3 [stage S1] Quality assurance scores by agent tenure band, April–July - QA team monthly scoring extract (system-record): Monthly sample of six calls per agent, scored by the QA team. Average score: April intake 81%; 6–24 months 87%; over 24 months 88%. Largest gaps for the intake: call opening and identity checks (−9 points), hold etiquette (−7). Billing calls only: intake 80%, tenured 86%. Intake scores rose each month, from 74% in April to 85% in July. The QA form scores process compliance and tone; it has no item for whether the customer's issue was resolved.
28	C4 [stage S1] Workforce management summary: headcount, occupancy, adherence, handle time, Jan–Jul - Resource Planning team (system-record): Phone headcount (FTE): Q1 average 201; May–Jul 208 (the April intake offset winter leavers). Occupancy: Q1 84.1%, May–Jul 86.9%. Schedule adherence: 91% → 90%. Abandonment rate: 4.2% → 5.1%. Average handle time: 6:52 → 7:14. Average speed of answer: 48s → 71s. Planner comment: 'Occupancy is higher than we'd like, but within the 85–88% band we planned for the summer.'
29	C5 [stage S1] HR attrition and sickness absence summary, Jan–Jul - HR business partner, Customer Operations (system-record): Agent leavers by month: Jan 6, Feb 5, Mar 7, Apr 4, May 5, Jun 6, Jul 5. Annualised attrition 34% (prior year 36%). Sickness absence: Q1 5.8%, May–Jul 4.9%. Exit interview themes (n=31): pay, shift patterns, commute. There have been no pay or grading changes this year. Two Billing Resolution team staff have been on long-term sick leave since May.
30	C6 [stage S1] MI repeat-contact analysis by contact reason, referral status and agent tenure, Jan–Jul - Management Information team (T. 32	C8 [stage S1] Interview with the Billing Resolution team manager - Notes of interview with Ade Fallon, Billing Resolution team manager, 7 August (manager-account): 'We've been swamped since spring. 33	C9 [stage S1] Knowledge base change log, 1 March–31 May - Knowledge Management team (log): 27 edits in the period. IVR section: menu map updated 28 Apr. Moving home: new direct-debit form link 9 May. The log records article, editor, date and a change summary. It does not record how often agents view each article.
34	C10 [stage S1] Post-call customer satisfaction survey results, Jan–Jul - Survey vendor monthly report (external-data): Post-call survey offered via IVR, 1–5 scale. Mean satisfaction: Jan 4.1, Feb 4.1, Mar 4.0, Apr 3.9, May 3.8, Jun 3.8, Jul 3.8. Response rate 6% of calls. Results are reported at site level only; the vendor's contract does not include breakdown by contact reason or agent. The question 'Would you need to contact us again about this?' was removed in January to shorten the survey.
35	C11 [stage S1] Finance Systems change record FC-0417 and associated sign-off notes - Finance Systems change register (change-record): Raised 2 Apr; implemented 14 Apr. Change: maximum credit adjustment a contact-centre agent can apply during a call reduced from £100 to £25 per account; the billing platform now blocks larger adjustments and automatically opens a referral to the Billing Resolution team. Reason: internal audit finding IA-11, unsupported goodwill and billing credits of £41,200 in Q4, 3.4% of agent-issued credit value. Impact assessment: 'Customer Operations impact minimal; system-enforced, no training required.' Reviewers: Finance Systems and Internal Audit; Customer Operations not consulted. The limit is a configuration parameter; changes take one working day.
36	C12 [stage S1] Team leader call-listening notes for the April intake, 12 May–20 June - Team leaders' coaching log (independent-observation): 48 calls reviewed. Common observations: long silences while searching screens; heavy reliance on hold; two calls transferred to a senior agent where the agent could have continued. Positives: accurate identity checks from week three; good empathy on tariff complaints. The log records coaching points only. Whether the customer contacted the centre again is not tracked in this log.
37	C13 [stage S1] Annual agent engagement survey results, June - People team survey report (anonymous-staff-survey): n=168 (79% response). Engagement index 61 (last year 66). Largest rise: 'My team leader supports me' 69% → 72%. Results are broken down by tenure only where a group exceeds 10 respondents with at least three months' service, so the April intake is not reported separately.
38	C14 [stage S1] Energy-retail contact centre benchmarking panel, H1 report - Contact Centre Benchmarking Forum (14 anonymised suppliers) (external-data): Median FCR across the panel: Q1 72%, Q2 71%. Thornlea's Q1 figure was in the top quartile. The report notes that member definitions vary (7- to 14-day windows; some count only same-reason repeats). Panel-wide call volumes rose 9% in April with spring tariff changes. No member-level detail is published.
39	C15 [stage S1] Customer Operations cost and overtime report, Jan–Jul - Finance business partner, Customer Operations (financial-record): Agent overtime hours: Q1 average 1,150 per month; May–Jul 1,420 per month. Agency staffing spend: nil throughout. Total cost per call: £4.62 in Q1, £4.71 in May–Jul. Year-to-date budget variance: +2.1%. Finance commentary: 'Overspend is driven by overtime to protect speed of answer.' No breakdown of cost by contact reason is held.
40	CANDIDATES
41	H1: The April intake of new agents, through their inexperience, caused the fall in FCR.
42	H2: The April Finance credit-handling controls update, by changing what agents could settle on the call, caused the fall in FCR.
43	H3: The April IVR menu redesign, by misrouting callers, caused the fall in FCR.
44	H4: Rising agent workload across the centre, by leaving agents too little time to resolve calls, caused the fall in FCR.
45	H5: The April tariff increase, by shifting the call mix toward contacts that are harder to resolve in one call, caused the fall in FCR.
46	R1: Finance credit-handling controls update FC-0417 (14 April) -> Rise in the share of billing calls referred to the Billing Resolution team (causes)
47	R2: Rise in the share of billing calls referred to the Billing Resolution team -> Fall in site FCR (causes)
48	R3: April intake going live on the phones (14 April) -> Fall in site FCR (causes)
49	R4: Fall in site FCR -> Rise in complaints per 10,000 contacts (causes)
50	A1: Agree with Finance a revised in-call credit authority for agents, backed by post-call sampling of credits; introduce it on two teams for six weeks and track FCR and the unsupported-credit rate before deciding on wider rollout.
51	A2: From September, put April-intake agents whose FCR is below 65% on performance-improvement plans, as the Head of Customer Operations proposes.
52	A3: Restore a higher in-call credit authority for all agents at once, backed by post-call sampling, without first trialling it on a limited group.
53	A4: Ask MI to rebuild the weekly FCR dashboard to add contact reason and referral status so future movements can be traced (MI estimate: about three months of one analyst's time, deferring other planned MI reports).
54	SCORED ITEMS

56	S02: hypothesis H2 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
57	S03: hypothesis H3 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
58	S04: hypothesis H4 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
59	S05: hypothesis H5 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
60	S06: edge R1 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
61	S07: edge R2 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
62	S08: edge R3 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
63	S09: edge R4 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
64	S10: action A1 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
65	S11: action A2 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
66	S12: action A3 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
67	S13: action A4 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
68	S14: sufficiency SUFF allowed=[sufficient, insufficient]

Reason: internal audit finding IA-11, unsupported goodwill and billing credits of £41,200 in Q4, 3.4% of agent-issued credit value. Impact assessment: 'Customer Operations impact minimal; system-enforced, no training required.' Reviewers: Finance Systems and Internal Audit; Customer Operations not consulted. Common observations: long silences while searching screens; heavy reliance on hold; two calls transferred to a senior agent where the agent could have continued. Positives: accurate identity checks from week three; good empathy on tariff complaints. The log records coaching points only. Whether the customer contacted the centre again is not tracked in this log.

Largest falls in agreement: 'I have the tools and authority to resolve customer problems' 71% → 52%; 'My workload is manageable' 58% → 49%; 'Changes are communicated well' 55% → 47%. Largest rise: 'My team leader supports me' 69% → 72%. Results are broken down by tenure only where a group exceeds 10 respondents with at least three months' service, so the April intake is not reported separately.

Thornlea's Q1 figure was in the top quartile. The report notes that member definitions vary (7- to 14-day windows; some count only same-reason repeats). Panel-wide call volumes rose 9% in April with spring tariff changes. No member-level detail is published.
C15 [stage S1] Customer Operations cost and overtime report, Jan–Jul - Finance business partner, Customer Operations (financial-record): Agent overtime hours: Q1 average 1,150 per month; May–Jul 1,420 per month. Agency staffing spend: nil throughout. Total cost per call: £4.62 in Q1, £4.71 in May–Jul. Year-to-date budget variance: +2.1%. Finance commentary: 'Overspend is driven by overtime to protect speed of answer.' No breakdown of cost by contact reason is held.

H1: The April intake of new agents, through their inexperience, caused the fall in FCR.
H2: The April Finance credit-handling controls update, by changing what agents could settle on the call, caused the fall in FCR.
H3: The April IVR menu redesign, by misrouting callers, caused the fall in FCR.
H4: Rising agent workload across the centre, by leaving agents too little time to resolve calls, caused the fall in FCR.
H5: The April tariff increase, by shifting the call mix toward contacts that are harder to resolve in one call, caused the fall in FCR.
R1: Finance credit-handling controls update FC-0417 (14 April) -> Rise in the share of billing calls referred to the Billing Resolution team (causes)
R2: Rise in the share of billing calls referred to the Billing Resolution team -> Fall in site FCR (causes)
R3: April intake going live on the phones (14 April) -> Fall in site FCR (causes)
R4: Fall in site FCR -> Rise in complaints per 10,000 contacts (causes)
A1: Agree with Finance a revised in-call credit authority for agents, backed by post-call sampling of credits; introduce it on two teams for six weeks and track FCR and the unsupported-credit rate before deciding on wider rollout.

A3: Restore a higher in-call credit authority for all agents at once, backed by post-call sampling, without first trialling it on a limited group.

answers.justification: C6 shows tenured agents' FCR fell just as far (75.1→67.3 and 75.0→67.2) as the April intake's 66.4%, and billing referral rates were similar by tenure (56/54/53%). C1 and C3 show a normal cohort, so the intake does not explain the site fall.

FC-0417 cut the in-call credit limit from £100 to £25 and auto-opens BRT referrals (C11). Billing referrals jumped from 7% to 54% in w/c 14 Apr (C6), while referred FCR (~33%) and non-referred FCR (82%) stayed flat. That shift in billing calls alone takes billing FCR from 79% to 56% and accounts for the whole ~8-point site drop, since other contact reasons were unchanged (C6, E2).

The IVR went live on 28 Apr, after FCR had already fallen in w/c 14 and 21 Apr (E2, E3). The misrouting proxy did not worsen (3.8% vs 4.0%, C2), and FCR within non-billing contact reasons did not move (C6).

Occupancy and handle time rose only modestly (C4), but FCR held steady for payments, moving home, meter calls and non-referred billing calls (C6). A centre-wide workload effect would have lowered those too, so the extra workload looks like a result of repeat contacts rather than a cause.

Tariff calls doubled their share (6%→12%), but they have high FCR (86→85%, C6), so that mix shift would push site FCR up, not down. FCR was also flat in the first two weeks after the 1 April increase (E2: 75.1%, 74.8%).

FC-0417 makes the system block adjustments over £25 and automatically open a BRT referral (C11). Referrals stepped up exactly in w/c 14 Apr (C6), equally across tenure bands, which rules out the intake as the rival explanation, and BRT says much of the new work is small adjustments (C8).

Referred billing calls resolve at ~33% against a stable 82% for non-referred calls (C6), and 58% of sampled repeat contacts after a referral were chasing its status (C6). The rise in referrals arithmetically accounts for the whole site drop, while every other reason's FCR stayed flat.

The intake's FCR (66.4%) is barely different from tenured agents (67.2–67.3%), and the tenured bands fell by the same 8 points (C6). The shared start date of 14 Apr (E3) is a coincidence, not a cause.

Complaints rose from 41 to 47–50 per 10,000 at the same time as the FCR drop (E5). However, complaints are not linked to the originating call and 64% are uncategorised (E5), so causation cannot be established.

A1 targets the cause identified in C6/C11 and meets the financial controller's stated condition (a compensating control proven on a limited population, C11). The limit is a one-day configuration change, and MI can track the trial teams within a day (C6).

The intake agents perform like tenured agents (C6), so putting them on performance plans would punish the wrong group (E6) and leave the referral cause untouched; with site FCR around 67%, many agents across all tenures would fall below the 65% cut-off.

A3 may well be the right end state, but Finance requires post-call sampling to be shown on a limited population to keep unsupported credits below 1% first (C11, IA-11 £41,200 finding), and that is not yet established.

Better visibility of contact reason and referral status is reasonable given the dashboard's blind spots (E2), but MI can already rerun the breakdown within a day (C6). That makes three months of analyst time a lower priority than fixing the credit limit.
C6's decomposition by contact reason, referral status and tenure, together with C11's mechanism and timing, is enough to commit to the limited, monitored trial in A1.

ambiguousItems: S12: premature vs harmful — rolling out everywhere at once goes ahead of Finance's evidence condition on a protective audit control (C11), but it is backed by sampling, so 'harmful' is arguable rather than clear.
S13: acceptable vs premature — the item depends on no hypothesis, but its cost and the fact that a one-day MI rerun already exists (C6) could push it lower.
S07: causal vs association-only — the evidence is observational, but the stratification and the C6 repeat-contact sample make a causal reading strong.
S09: association-only vs causal — the timing and the 'Service – delay' category hint at a mechanism, but complaints are not linked to the originating call.
caseProblems: C6 settles almost the whole case in one item: the decomposition by reason, referral and tenure answers H1–H5 and R1–R3 together. That makes the case easy once C6 is collected, and its title ('by contact reason, referral status and agent tenure') signals how useful it is.
C11's financial controller's note (30 Jul) almost word-for-word describes A1 (a compensating control on a limited population), which leaks the preferred action.

Minor inconsistency: C8 says BRT turnaround roughly doubled (3 → 6–7 working days) and two staff are on long-term sick (C5), yet C6 reports referred-call FCR unchanged or slightly better (33% → 34%) under a 7-day window. A longer backlog would be expected to lower referred FCR.
C6 figures reconcile exactly (billing 0.07×33+0.93×82≈79; 0.54×34+0.46×82≈56; site ≈75.0 → 67.1), which is good internal consistency but rather tidy for real MI data.
